items.title: The Four Buddhist Councils (I–IV)
items.body:
## Why Councils Were Held

**In one line:** After the Buddha's death his followers held four great Councils to fix the teachings, and the religion later split into schools (Hinayana, Mahayana, Vajrayana) that produced distinct art, texts and architecture.

**Why it is asked:** Councils (place, king, president), the school-wise contrasts, and Buddhist art/architecture are dense fact clusters that examiners love to scramble in match-the-pairs questions.

**The story**

After the Buddha's *Mahaparinirvana*, monks assembled in **Councils (Sangitis)** to **compile his teachings**, **settle disputes over monastic discipline**, and **preserve doctrinal purity**. Each council had a **venue**, a **royal patron**, and a **presiding monk**.

## The Four Councils

| Council | Venue | Patron (King) | President | Key Outcome |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **1st (483 BCE)** | **Rajagriha** | **Ajatashatru** | **Mahakassapa** | Compiled the **Vinaya Pitaka** (recited by Upali) and **Sutta Pitaka** (recited by Ananda). |
| **2nd (383 BCE)** | **Vaishali** | **Kalashoka** | **Sabbakami** | Addressed **corruption in the Sangha** and reaffirmed **monastic discipline**. |
| **3rd (250 BCE)** | **Pataliputra** | **Ashoka** | **Moggaliputta Tissa** | **Theravada** established; compiled the **Abhidhamma Pitaka**; **missionaries** sent abroad; Ashoka later raised **84,000 stupas**. |
| **4th (1st century CE)** | **Kashmir** | **Kanishka** | **Vasumitra** (deputy **Ashvaghosha**) | Division into **Mahayana** and **Hinayana**; **Sanskrit** became the language of scriptures. |

## Significance

- The councils progressively fixed the **Tripitaka** (Three Baskets).
- The **4th** council marks the great split into **Mahayana** and **Hinayana**.
- Royal patronage (**Ajatashatru → Kanishka**) shows how the **state** repeatedly sustained the Sangha.

**TL;DR**

- 1st Council — Rajagriha, patron Ajatashatru, president Mahakassapa: compiled Vinaya & Sutta Pitakas.
- 2nd Council — Vaishali, patron Kalashoka, president Sabbakami: addressed Sangha corruption; reaffirmed discipline.
- 3rd Council — Pataliputra, patron Ashoka, president Moggaliputta Tissa: Theravada established; Abhidhamma Pitaka; missionaries dispatched.
- 4th Council — Kashmir, patron Kanishka, president Vasumitra: Mahayana–Hinayana division; canon in Sanskrit.
- Councils fixed the Tripitaka and defined Buddhism's major schools.
keyPoints: 1st Council — Rajagriha, patron Ajatashatru, president Mahakassapa: compiled Vinaya & Sutta Pitakas.
2nd Council — Vaishali, patron Kalashoka, president Sabbakami: addressed Sangha corruption; reaffirmed discipline.
3rd Council — Pataliputra, patron Ashoka, president Moggaliputta Tissa: Theravada established; Abhidhamma Pitaka; missionaries dispatched.
4th Council — Kashmir, patron Kanishka, president Vasumitra: Mahayana–Hinayana division; canon in Sanskrit.
Councils fixed the Tripitaka and defined Buddhism's major schools.

items.title: Schools of Buddhism, Bodhisattvas & Spread
items.body:
## Hinayana (Theravada)

**In one line** — Hinayana (Theravada) = 'Lesser Path'; Buddha as human, no idols, Pali scriptures, Nirvana; patron Ashoka; Sri Lanka/Myanmar/Thailand.

**The story**

- **'The Lesser Path'**; *Theravada* = **'Doctrine of the Elders'** — follows the **original teachings** of the Buddha.
- Views the **Buddha as a human**, **discourages idol worship**, and stresses **self-discipline and meditation** for **individual salvation (Nirvana)**.
- Scriptures in **Pali**; practised today in **Sri Lanka, Myanmar, Thailand**. **Ashoka** was its great patron.

## Mahayana

- **'The Greater Path'**; arose **later** and is a **heterodox** school.
- Treats the **Buddha as divine**, permits **idol worship** of the Buddha and **Bodhisattvas**, and believes in **universal liberation** for all beings.
- Scriptures in **Sanskrit**; emphasises **mantras**; practised in **Japan and China**. **Kanishka** was its notable patron.

## Vajrayana

- **'Vehicle of the Thunderbolt'**, i.e. **Tantric Buddhism**; upholds the **Two Truths Doctrine** (conventional & ultimate).
- Uses **symbolic language (*Sandhya-bhasa*)**, worships fierce deities like **Tara**, and centres on the **Guru (Lama)**.
- Arose in **Bengal and Bihar**, gained prominence in the **11th century**; popular in **Tibet, Nepal, Bhutan, Mongolia**.

## The Bodhisattva Ideal

- A **Bodhisattva** is an **enlightened being who postpones personal Nirvana** to help **all beings attain liberation** — the moral core of **Mahayana**, contrasting with Hinayana's focus on **individual salvation**.

## Spread & Decline

- Carried by **royal patrons** — **Ashoka, Kanishka, Satavahanas, Rashtrakutas, Chalukyas** — Buddhism spread across and beyond India.
- Its **decline** in India followed the **revival of Brahmanism**, **loss of royal patronage**, growing **ritualism (Vajrayana)**, and **later invasions** that destroyed monasteries.

## Don't confuse
- **Hinayana vs Mahayana vs Vajrayana:** Hinayana (Theravada) uses **Pali** texts and was promoted by **Ashoka**; Mahayana uses **Sanskrit**, worships the Buddha as god and was promoted by **Kanishka**; Vajrayana is the later **Tantric** path using magical rituals.
- **Language cue:** Pali = Hinayana, Sanskrit = Mahayana — the fastest way to tell an option apart.

**TL;DR**

- Hinayana (Theravada) = 'Lesser Path'; Buddha as human, no idols, Pali scriptures, Nirvana; patron Ashoka; Sri Lanka/Myanmar/Thailand.
- Mahayana = 'Greater Path'; Buddha divine, idol & Bodhisattva worship, Sanskrit, mantras; patron Kanishka; Japan/China.
- Vajrayana = 'Vehicle of the Thunderbolt' (Tantric); Sandhya-bhasa, Tara, Guru/Lama; arose in Bengal-Bihar (11th c.); Tibet/Nepal/Bhutan.
- Bodhisattva = enlightened being who defers Nirvana to liberate all beings — the Mahayana ideal.
- Royal patrons: Ashoka, Kanishka, Satavahanas, Rashtrakutas, Chalukyas.
- Decline: Brahmanical revival, lost patronage, ritualism, and invasions.
- Mahasanghika's deification of the Buddha seeded Mahayana; the Sthaviravadins (Theravada) belonged to Hinayana, not Mahayana.

Mahayana = 'Greater Path'; Buddha divine, idol & Bodhisattva worship, Sanskrit, mantras; patron Kanishka; Japan/China.
Vajrayana = 'Vehicle of the Thunderbolt' (Tantric); Sandhya-bhasa, Tara, Guru/Lama; arose in Bengal-Bihar (11th c.); Tibet/Nepal/Bhutan.

items.title: Buddhist Literature: The Tripitaka & Centres of Learning
items.body:
## The Tripitaka (Three Baskets)

**In one line** — Tripitaka = Vinaya (discipline) + Sutta (sermons) + Abhidhamma (philosophy).

**The story**

Buddhist religious literature is collectively the **Tripitaka**:

- **Vinaya Pitaka** — **rules of discipline** for monks and nuns.
- **Sutta Pitaka** — **sermons and stories** of the Buddha.
- **Abhidhamma Pitaka** — **philosophical and metaphysical** discussions.

## Other Famous Texts

- **Dighanikaya**, **Nirgrantha**, the **Jataka tales** (stories of the Buddha's previous births), **Therigatha**, and **Ashvaghosha's *Buddhacharita*** advanced the spread and understanding of Buddhism.

## Centres of Learning

- Buddhist **monasteries became centres of learning**, growing into great universities: **Nalanda, Taxila, Valabhi, and Vikramasila** — magnets for scholars from across the world.

**TL;DR**

- Tripitaka = Vinaya (discipline) + Sutta (sermons) + Abhidhamma (philosophy).
- Vinaya Pitaka governs monastic rules; Sutta Pitaka holds the Buddha's discourses; Abhidhamma is metaphysical analysis.
- Key texts: Dighanikaya, Nirgrantha, Jataka tales, Therigatha, Ashvaghosha's Buddhacharita.
- Jataka tales narrate the Buddha's previous births and are a rich source of early Indian social history.
- Buddhist universities: Nalanda, Taxila, Valabhi, Vikramasila.
- Most Hinayana canon is in Pali; Mahayana texts are largely in Sanskrit.

figure.caption: Monastic universities — Nalanda, Taxila and Vikramshila — grew out of Buddhist monasteries.

items.title: Buddhist Art & Architecture: Stupa, Chaitya, Vihara
items.body:
## Sculptural Schools

**In one line** — Sculptural schools: Gandhara (Greco-Roman), Mathura (indigenous, yakshas), Amaravati (narrative carvings).

**The story**

- **Gandhara art** — **Greco-Roman** influence; realistic Buddha sculptures.
- **Mathura art** — indigenous Indian style; Buddha images and **yakshas**.
- **Amaravati school** — delicate carvings and **narrative** sculpture.

## Stupa, Chaitya, Vihara

- **Stupa** — a **hemispherical shrine** housing **relics** of the Buddha; famous examples: **Sanchi** and **Bharhut**.
- **Chaitya** — a **prayer hall**; **Vihara** — a **monastery** where monks resided.
- **Rock-cut caves** at **Ajanta, Ellora and Bhaja** served as monasteries and worship halls, adorned with murals and sculpture.

## The Five Elements of a Stupa

- **Base (square)** → Earth · **Dome/anda (hemisphere)** → Water · **Harmika (platform)** → Fire · **Yasti (central pole)** → Air · **Chattras (umbrella/spire)** → Space.
- Origin: evolved from **burial mounds** (6th century BCE); **Ashoka** popularised stupas, raising **84,000** after the **3rd Council**.

## Pillars & Famous Stupas

- The **Sarnath Pillar** of **Ashoka** bears the **Lion Capital** — now India's **national emblem**.
- Great stupas: **Sanchi** (India), **Boudhanath** & **Mahabodhi**, **Shwedagon** (Myanmar). Regional forms: **dagobas** (Sri Lanka), **chortens** (Tibet), **pagodas** (East Asia).

**TL;DR**

- Sculptural schools: Gandhara (Greco-Roman), Mathura (indigenous, yakshas), Amaravati (narrative carvings).
- Stupa = relic shrine; Chaitya = prayer hall; Vihara = monastery.
- Stupa's five elements: Base=Earth, Dome=Water, Harmika=Fire, Yasti=Air, Chattras=Space.
- Rock-cut caves: Ajanta, Ellora, Bhaja. Famous stupas: Sanchi, Bharhut, Mahabodhi.
- Ashoka raised 84,000 stupas after the 3rd Council; his Sarnath Lion Capital is India's national emblem.
- Regional stupa forms: dagobas (Sri Lanka), chortens (Tibet), pagodas (East Asia).
- Kanganahalli (Sannati, Karnataka) yielded the 'Ranyo Ashoka' relief — a labelled sculpted portrait of Ashoka.

items.title: The Bodhisattva Ideal & the Eight Great Bodhisattvas
items.body:
## The Bodhisattva Concept

**In one line** — Bodhisattva = enlightened being who stays in samsara to help all beings reach enlightenment (Mahayana ideal).

**The story**

- **Bodhisattvas** are revered figures in **Mahayana** Buddhism — **enlightened beings who choose to remain in the cycle of *samsara*** to help others attain enlightenment, rather than pass into Nirvana themselves.
- Each embodies a specific virtue such as **wisdom, compassion, or power**, guiding devotees toward **spiritual liberation**. **Avalokiteshvara**, known for compassion, is worshipped across Buddhist cultures.

## The Eight Great Bodhisattvas

| Bodhisattva | Represents / Known for |
|---|---|
| **Manjushri** | **Wisdom** — depicted with a blazing sword cutting through ignorance. |
| **Avalokiteshvara** (Padmapani) | **Infinite compassion** — holds a lotus; linked to Buddha Amitabha. |
| **Vajrapani** | **Power and energy** of all Buddhas — warrior stance amid flames. |
| **Kshitigarbha** | Vow to **save all beings**, including those in hell and children who died young. |
| **Akashagarbha** | **Cleansing of sins** and granting of wisdom. |
| **Samantabhadra** | **Ten vows** of ethical conduct and altruism. |
| **Sarvanivarana-Vishkambhin** | **Purification of obstacles** on the path. |
| **Maitreya** | The **future Buddha**, destined to restore the Dharma. |

**TL;DR**

- Bodhisattva = enlightened being who stays in samsara to help all beings reach enlightenment (Mahayana ideal).
- Manjushri = wisdom (blazing sword); Avalokiteshvara = infinite compassion (lotus).
- Vajrapani = power of all Buddhas; Kshitigarbha = vow to save beings in hell.
- Akashagarbha = cleanses sins; Samantabhadra = ten vows; Sarvanivarana-Vishkambhin = purifies obstacles.
- Maitreya = the future Buddha who will restore the teachings.
- Paramitas — the perfections (e.g., dana, sila, kshanti, virya, dhyana, prajna) a Bodhisattva cultivates toward Buddhahood.

items.title: Spread of Buddhism & Its Royal Patrons
items.body:
## How Buddhism Spread

**In one line** — Spread by the missionary Sangha; the Buddha taught in Prakrit, the people's language.

**The story**

- Buddhism spread rapidly across **North India** during the Buddha's lifetime and beyond, driven by the **missionary activity of the Sangha** and preaching in **Prakrit**, the language of the masses.
- **Emperor Ashoka** was pivotal to its **global expansion**: after the **Kalinga War** he embraced Buddhism and sent **missionaries** to **Sri Lanka, Greece, Myanmar, Thailand and Central Asia**.
- **Ashoka's Edicts** — inscriptions across and beyond India — promoted the Buddha's teachings and outlined the **Dhamma** (moral code).

## Royal Patrons

- **Ashoka** — institutionalised Buddhism via the **3rd Council**, edicts and missionaries; patron of **Hinayana/Theravada**.
- **Kanishka** — championed **Mahayana** at the **4th Council**, enabling its **Central and East Asian** diffusion.
- **Satavahanas, Rashtrakutas and Chalukyas** — supported Buddhist **architecture and monasteries**.

## Survival Beyond India

- Despite decline in India, Buddhism **flourished in East Asia** (China, Japan) and **Southeast Asia** (Thailand, Myanmar, Sri Lanka).

**TL;DR**

- Spread by the missionary Sangha; the Buddha taught in Prakrit, the people's language.
- Ashoka embraced Buddhism after the Kalinga War and sent missionaries to Sri Lanka, Greece, Myanmar, Thailand and Central Asia.
- Ashoka's Edicts promoted the Dhamma across and beyond India.
- Royal patrons: Ashoka (Hinayana), Kanishka (Mahayana), Satavahanas, Rashtrakutas, Chalukyas.
- Buddhism survived and flourished in East and Southeast Asia after declining in India.

items.title: Causes of the Decline of Buddhism in India
items.body:
## Internal Causes

**In one line** — Internal: corruption of the Sangha, rise of ritualism, and fragmentation into Hinayana/Mahayana/Vajrayana/Tantrayana sects.

**The story**

- **Corruption of the Sangha** — a drift from the Buddha's original discipline.
- **Rise of ritualistic practices** — especially under **Tantric/Vajrayana** forms, which blurred Buddhism's early simplicity.
- **Sectarian fragmentation** — the splitting of Buddhism into **Hinayana, Mahayana, Vajrayana and Tantrayana** sects weakened its unity.

## External Causes

- **Revival of Brahmanical Hinduism** — reabsorbed followers, aided by the **Bhakti** movement and the co-option of the Buddha as an *avatar*.
- **Loss of royal patronage** — as later kings favoured Brahmanism.
- **Muslim invasions of the 12th century CE** — led to the **destruction of monasteries** (e.g. Nalanda) and monks.

## Aftermath

- Buddhism **declined in the land of its birth** but **survived in Asia** — East Asia (China, Japan) and Southeast Asia (Thailand, Myanmar, Sri Lanka).

**TL;DR**

- Internal: corruption of the Sangha, rise of ritualism, and fragmentation into Hinayana/Mahayana/Vajrayana/Tantrayana sects.
- External: revival of Brahmanical Hinduism and the loss of royal patronage.
- Muslim invasions of the 12th century CE destroyed monasteries such as Nalanda.
- Buddhism declined in India but flourished in East and Southeast Asia.

items.title: Major Buddhist Sites & UNESCO World Heritage
items.body:
## UNESCO World Heritage Sites

**In one line** — Nalanda Mahavihara (Bihar) — Buddhist university, UNESCO 2016.

**The story**

Several Buddhist sites mark critical stages in the evolution of Buddhist architecture and religion:

| Site | Location | Significance | Inscribed |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Nalanda Mahavihara** | Nalanda, **Bihar** | Great centre of Buddhist studies (est. 5th c. CE) drawing scholars worldwide. | **2016** |
| **Buddhist Monuments at Sanchi** | **Madhya Pradesh** | **Sanchi Stupa** commissioned by **Ashoka** (3rd c. BCE); major pilgrimage site. | **1989** |
| **Mahabodhi Temple, Bodh Gaya** | **Bihar** | Where **Siddhartha attained enlightenment** under the Bodhi Tree. | **2002** |
| **Ajanta Caves** | Aurangabad, **Maharashtra** | Rock-cut cave temples with famous Buddhist **paintings and sculptures** (from c. 2nd c. BCE). | **1983** |

## Why They Matter

- Together they trace Buddhism's arc from **enlightenment (Bodh Gaya)** and **royal monument-building (Sanchi)** to **monastic scholarship (Nalanda)** and **rock-cut art (Ajanta)**.

**TL;DR**

- Nalanda Mahavihara (Bihar) — Buddhist university, UNESCO 2016.
- Sanchi (Madhya Pradesh) — Ashoka's stupa, UNESCO 1989.
- Mahabodhi Temple, Bodh Gaya (Bihar) — site of enlightenment, UNESCO 2002.
- Ajanta Caves (Maharashtra) — rock-cut Buddhist paintings, UNESCO 1983.
- The four sites span enlightenment, royal monuments, scholarship and cave art.

items.title: Stupas: Purpose, Types, Famous Examples & Regional Forms
items.body:
## Purpose & Origin

**In one line** — Stupa = hemispherical relic shrine symbolising the enlightened mind; evolved from burial mounds (6th c. BCE).

**The story**

- A **stupa** is a **hemispherical shrine** built to **house relics** of the Buddha or other significant figures; it **symbolises the enlightened mind** and is linked to meditation.
- The tradition **originated in India**, evolving from **burial mounds** in the **6th century BCE**. **Ashoka** popularised stupa-building, reputedly raising **84,000** stupas after the **3rd Council**.

## Types of Stupas

- **Relic Stupas** — enshrine relics of the Buddha or his disciples.
- **Object Stupas** — contain sacred objects representing the teachings.
- **Commemorative Stupas** — mark important events in the Buddha's life.
- **Symbolic Stupas** — represent aspects of Buddhist theology (e.g. enlightenment).
- **Votive Stupas** — erected by devotees as devotion or to mark a pilgrimage.

## Famous Stupas

- **Sanchi** (Madhya Pradesh) — one of the oldest, built by **Ashoka**.
- **Boudhanath** (Kathmandu, Nepal) — a great centre of **Tibetan** Buddhism.
- **Shwedagon** (Yangon, Myanmar) — most sacred pagoda in Myanmar.
- **Mahabodhi** (Bodh Gaya) — at the site of the Buddha's **enlightenment**.

## Regional Forms

- **Dagobas** (Sri Lanka) · **Chortens** (Tibet, multi-tiered) · **Pagodas** (East Asia, tall tiered towers).

**TL;DR**

- Stupa = hemispherical relic shrine symbolising the enlightened mind; evolved from burial mounds (6th c. BCE).
- Ashoka reputedly raised 84,000 stupas after the 3rd Council.
- Five types: Relic, Object, Commemorative, Symbolic, Votive.
- Famous: Sanchi (India), Boudhanath (Nepal), Shwedagon (Myanmar), Mahabodhi (Bodh Gaya).
- Regional forms: dagobas (Sri Lanka), chortens (Tibet), pagodas (East Asia).

items.title: Mudras in Buddhist Art & the Dhyani Buddhas
items.body:
## What Mudras Are

**In one line** — Mudras are symbolic hand gestures, each tied to a Dhyani (meditation) Buddha.

**The story**

- **Mudras** are **symbolic hand gestures** in Buddhist iconography, each carrying a distinct meaning and often associated with a **Dhyani (meditation) Buddha**.

## The Principal Mudras

| Mudra | Meaning | Dhyani Buddha |
|---|---|---|
| **Dharmachakra** | 'Wheel of Dharma' — teaching | **Vairochana** (first) |
| **Bhumisparsha** | 'Touching the soil' — the **earth-witness** | **Akshobhya** (second) |
| **Varada** | **Kindness, compassion, blessing** | **Ratnasambhava** (third) |
| **Dhyana** | **Meditation** (one or both hands) | **Amitabha / Amitayus** (fourth) |
| **Abhaya** | **Fearlessness**, safety, removal of fear | **Amoghasiddhi** |

## Why It Matters

- Recognising mudras helps **identify Buddha images** in sculpture and painting across the Gandhara, Mathura and Amaravati traditions.

**TL;DR**

- Mudras are symbolic hand gestures, each tied to a Dhyani (meditation) Buddha.
- Dharmachakra (teaching) → Vairochana; Bhumisparsha (earth-witness) → Akshobhya.
- Varada (blessing) → Ratnasambhava; Dhyana (meditation) → Amitabha.
- Abhaya (fearlessness) → Amoghasiddhi.
- Mudras help identify Buddha images across sculptural schools.

items.title: For Mains — Buddhism II (Councils, Schools & Art)
items.body:
## How Mains frames the councils, schools and art

Mains (Paper-II, clause M2-1, with overlap into Art & Culture) asks you to *trace evolution* — how a monastic community fractured into schools and became a civilisational force in art and diplomacy. Organise answers around **doctrinal change → royal patronage → cultural output**.

| Dimension | Analytical thrust |
|---|---|
| Councils | Each council codified canon and widened fault-lines (II = Ten Points; IV = Mahayana/Hinayana) |
| Schools | Hinayana (human Buddha, Pali) → Mahayana (Bodhisattva, Sanskrit, image-worship) → Vajrayana (Tantra) |
| Patronage | Ashoka (institutionalised, missionaries) and Kanishka (Mahayana, Gandhara art) as hinge figures |
| Art/architecture | Stupa–chaitya–vihara; Gandhara/Mathura/Amaravati schools; rock-cut Ajanta/Ellora |
| Decline & legacy | Brahmanical revival + 12th-c. invasions vs enduring Asian cultural diplomacy |

**Data points / anchors to quote:** 4 Councils (Rajagriha 483 BCE → Kashmir c.72 CE); Ashoka's 84,000 stupas & Third Council (Moggaliputta Tissa, Kathavatthu); Kanishka + Ashvaghosha/Vasumitra; UNESCO sites Sanchi (1989), Ajanta (1983), Mahabodhi (2002), Nalanda (2016); the Nalanda revival as modern soft-power (2016 inscription, international university).

**AP angle (high value):** The **Amaravati** school of white-marble sculpture (Satavahana–Ikshvaku) is a world-class Buddhist art tradition on the Krishna; **Nagarjunakonda** was a great mahavihara and the seat of **Acharya Nagarjuna** (Madhyamaka/Shunyavada); **Bhattiprolu** yielded the earliest Brahmi relic-casket inscriptions and a casket of Buddha relics; **Kanganahalli** (just over the border) carries the 'Ranyo Ashoka' portrait. AP was effectively a second heartland of Buddhism.

**Use in answers:**
- *Thesis line:* "The councils turned a Sangha into a canon; patronage turned a canon into an empire of ideas and art."
- *Diagram idea:* a timeline band — 4 councils above, 3 schools branching below, art schools as leaves.
- *Quote:* Nagarjuna's Shunyavada ('emptiness') as India's gift to Mahayana philosophy.
- Conclude with Buddhism's role in India's Act-East cultural diplomacy today.
keyPoints: Structure answers as doctrinal change → royal patronage → cultural output.
Councils both codified canon and widened schisms (II Ten Points; IV Mahayana split).
Ashoka and Kanishka are the hinge patrons; cite 84,000 stupas and the Gandhara school.
Art: stupa/chaitya/vihara + Gandhara/Mathura/Amaravati; UNESCO Sanchi, Ajanta, Nalanda.
AP angle: Amaravati, Nagarjunakonda (Acharya Nagarjuna), Bhattiprolu as a Buddhist heartland.
items.source: R.S. Sharma, India's Ancient Past; A.L. Basham, The Wonder That Was India; ASI Amaravati/Nagarjunakonda
